articles.title: Before you submit your MCP server to Claude's Connectors Directory: a checklist from Anthropic's own review criteria
articles.excerpt: I have two MCP servers waiting in the Connectors Directory review queue right now, so I went through Anthropic's published criteria line by line and turned them into a checklist. Everything below come…
articles.body: I have two MCP servers waiting in the Connectors Directory review queue right now, so I went through Anthropic's published criteria line by line and turned them into a checklist. Everything below comes from the official docs (links at the end). I do not know the inside of the review, only what Anthropic publishes, and I cannot promise acceptance for anyone, including myself. Split read and write tools. A single tool that accepts both safe HTTP methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) and unsafe ones (POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) is rejected. No catch-all api_request tool with a method parameter. Writing "safe versus unsafe" in the description does not count; the operations must be separate tools, ideally split further into create, update and delete. Annotate every tool.

articles.title: Trading Crypto Across Time Zones: How a Market That Never Closes Breaks the Indicator Assumptions Built for Stocks
articles.excerpt: Somewhere around 3 a.m. local time, a trader who has spent years in equities watches a Bitcoin position get stopped out on what looks like noise. The RSI(14) reading that would have meant something on…
articles.body: Somewhere around 3 a.m. local time, a trader who has spent years in equities watches a Bitcoin position get stopped out on what looks like noise. The RSI(14) reading that would have meant something on a liquid NYSE afternoon just meant very little on a thin overnight candle in a market with almost nobody awake to trade it. Nothing about the indicator was broken. The assumption baked into it — that price action reflects a reasonably liquid, actively-traded session — simply wasn't true at that hour, on that chart. This is the quiet problem with moving a stock-trained indicator stack onto crypto unmodified. Most of the technical toolkit traders use was developed, tested, and tuned against markets that open, close, and pause. Crypto does none of those things.

articles.title: Mounting a Local USB Drive to a Cloud VPS Securely with SSHFS and a Chroot Jail
articles.excerpt: Cloud VPS instances are great for compute, testing, and always-on development environments—until you start running low on disk space or want to work with large local files directly from your cloud wor…
articles.body: Cloud VPS instances are great for compute, testing, and always-on development environments—until you start running low on disk space or want to work with large local files directly from your cloud workspace without uploading gigabytes over the internet every time. Instead of paying for extra block storage, you can bridge an external USB drive plugged into your local Ubuntu-based workstation straight to any cloud VPS using a reverse SSH tunnel and SSHFS . Even better: with a few OpenSSH lockdown rules, you can ensure that even if your VPS were ever compromised, an attacker would be strictly trapped inside your USB drive with zero shell access, zero port forwarding, and zero visibility into your local home directory.

articles.body: Originally published at muhammadmoiz.dev . To build an MVP without wasting six months, start from one painful problem and one type of customer, write down the single job your product must do, cut every feature that doesn't serve that job, and put a working version in front of real users within weeks rather than quarters. Anything you can do by hand behind the scenes, do by hand at first. The goal of a minimum viable product is learning what customers will actually use and pay for, not shipping a smaller copy of your dream app. This guide walks through how to create an MVP step by step, how to decide what to cut, and the mistakes that turn a six-week project into a six-month one. articles.title: Check for source overlap before you trust an ML test score
articles.excerpt: A dataset can have unique row IDs and still leak. For example, a microscopy image might be exported as several crops. A row-level random split can then put crops from the same source image in both tra…
articles.body: A dataset can have unique row IDs and still leak. For example, a microscopy image might be exported as several crops. A row-level random split can then put crops from the same source image in both train and test. The experiment would measure performance on partly familiar sources. Keep a group ID that reflects the unit you want to generalize to. Depending on your study, that might be the original image, device, site, or participant. Decide which unit matters before assigning splits. For prospective use, record the time cutoff as well. Here is a runnable Python check using synthetic split rows. It prints every overlapping source ID and flags which splits share it.

articles.title: This supernova impostor baffled astronomers for 15 years — until they found a hidden black hole feeding on an unstable star
articles.excerpt: A hidden black hole or neutron star companion to an unstable massive star is causing the system to erupt in light that mimics a supernova explosion.
articles.body: A cosmic imposter that has faked being a supernova 27 times and counting is actually a hot, luminous, and decidedly unstable star that is being fed on by a vampiric black hole or neutron star, NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory has discovered. When a massive star reaches the end of the road and runs out of nuclear fuel to power fusion reactions in its core, the star is destroyed in a supernova explosion. That’s what astronomers thought they had found on 11 January 2012, when they observed what appeared to be a supernova on the outskirts of the spiral galaxy NGC 4559, which is about 25 million light-years away in the constellation Coma Berenices. Yet when the light of the 'supernova' faded, the star was still there, only to continue bursting into light every 113 days.

articles.excerpt: On Nov. 12, 2014, a European spacecraft named Philae landed on Comet 67P, then bounced twice and got lost. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 12, 2014, a European spacecraft named Philae landed on Comet 67P . To say it was a bumpy landing would be an understatement. The European Space Agency's Philae lander separated from an orbiter called Rosetta ahead of its historic landing in 2014. It was supposed to use harpoons to secure itself on to the surface of Comet 67P, but the harpoons never fired. When it touched down, it immediately bounced back up into space . The first bounce brought Philae half a mile above the comet's surface before gravity brought it back down. Philae was missing for almost two years before scientists found it . Images from Rosetta showed Philae stuck in a dark crevice on top of the rubber duck-shaped comet.

articles.title: Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility
articles.excerpt: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT…
articles.body: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.” Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China.

articles.excerpt: For Katie Spicer, embracing opportunity and challenge has led to giant leaps during her time at NASA. Now as the NASA lander integration lead for Blue Origin’s Blue Moon Mark 2 lander, one of the comm…
articles.body: 4 Min Read I Am Artemis Katie Spicer For Katie Spicer, embracing opportunity and challenge has led to giant leaps during her time at NASA. Now as the NASA lander integration lead for Blue Origin’s Blue Moon Mark 2 lander, one of the commercially provided human landing systems for NASA’s Artemis program, Spicer will have her handprint on history. NASA’s Katie Spicer stands in front of the crew cabin prototype for Blue Origin’s Blue Moon Mark 2 lunar lander. The lander is one of two commercial human landing systems that will help safely ferry astronauts from lunar orbit to the Moon’s surface and back for the agency’s crewed Artemis missions in 2028.
